title: Tool Users of the Kelp Forest

passage.title: Tool Users of the Kelp Forest
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
Cold waves roll across the giant kelp forests that grow along the Pacific coast. Unlike seals and whales, sea otters do not have a thick layer of blubber. Instead, they rely on the thickest fur coat in the animal kingdom. Up to a million hairs pack into a single square inch of skin. This dense fur traps a layer of dry air right against their skin as they swim. In addition, sea otters must eat a fourth of their body weight every day to stay warm.

To find that much food, otters dive down to the murky bottom. There they forage for crabs, clams, and spiny sea urchins. Most ocean hunters cannot bite through the tough armor of a clam or urchin without breaking their teeth. Sea otters solve this problem by using stone tools. Along the rocky coast, the hard purple shells gathered from the sea floor are cracked by hungry otters using flat anvil stones. Floating on its back, an otter sets a smooth rock on its chest. Then it taps the shell against the stone until it splits open.

Each sea otter even has a built-in tool bag under its front leg. Loose folds of skin under the left armpit form a deep pocket that can hold a favorite rock from dive to dive. The otter also tucks extra clams into this pouch so it can carry several snacks to the surface at once.

After a long afternoon of diving, sea otters need a safe place to rest on the water. If they simply closed their eyes, strong ocean currents could sweep a sleeping otter far out to sea. To stay in one spot, otters drape long ribbons of floating giant kelp across their bellies like seat belts. These tough green blades anchor the sleeping animals above the reef until morning. Sometimes a dozen otters hold paws and float together in a cozy group.

This partnership helps the kelp forest just as much as it helps the otters. Hungry sea urchins love to chew through the bottom stems of giant kelp plants. Left alone, they can wipe out whole underwater forests. By eating thousands of urchins every week, sea otters play a vital role in protecting the green kelp canopy for fish, crabs, and seals.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Along the rocky coast, the hard purple shells gathered from the sea floor are cracked by hungry otters using flat anvil stones."

Who or what performs the action of cracking the hard purple shells in this sentence?

options.text: The sea floor along the rocky coast
options.childFeedback: The sea floor is just the bottom of the ocean where the shells were gathered; the ocean floor cannot crack shells.

options.text: The purple shells that were gathered during the dive
options.childFeedback: The hard purple shells are what get cracked open ('the hard purple shells... are cracked'), not the animals doing the cracking.

options.text: The hungry otters using flat anvil stones
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'are cracked by hungry otters using flat anvil stones' shows that the hungry otters perform the action of cracking the hard purple shells.

options.text: The seals and whales swimming through the kelp
options.childFeedback: Seals and whales are mentioned only in Paragraph 1 and Paragraph 5; Paragraph 2 states that hungry otters crack the shells with stones.

questions.provingSentenceText: Along the rocky coast, the hard purple shells gathered from the sea floor are cracked by hungry otters using flat anvil stones.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'are cracked by hungry otters using flat anvil stones' shows that the hungry otters perform the action of cracking the hard purple shells.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'the hard purple shells' receive the action of being cracked. The true actors are 'hungry otters,' introduced after the preposition 'by.'
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'cracked by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see who breaks open the purple shells.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"These tough green blades anchor the sleeping animals above the reef until morning."

What does the word "anchor" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Hold firmly in one place
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'anchor' means to hold firmly in one place, because wrapping in floating kelp blades keeps sleeping otters from being swept out to sea by strong currents.

options.text: Pull deep under the water
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says the kelp ribbons float and hold the sleeping animals 'above the reef,' not pull them deep underwater.

options.text: Feed snacks to during the night
options.childFeedback: The otters have already finished their afternoon of diving for food and are sleeping until morning, not eating snacks.

options.text: Hide from every wave forever
options.childFeedback: Floating on the water wrapped in kelp holds the otter in one spot above the reef, rather than hiding it from every ocean wave forever.

questions.provingSentenceText: These tough green blades anchor the sleeping animals above the reef until morning.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'anchor' means to hold firmly in one place, because wrapping in floating kelp blades keeps sleeping otters from being swept out to sea by strong currents.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that otters wrap themselves in floating kelp like seat belts so ocean currents cannot sweep them out to sea. Thus, 'anchor' means to hold firmly in place.
questions.retryHint: Read the two sentences right before this one in Paragraph 4 to see how wrapping in kelp like a seat belt helps a sleeping otter stay in one spot.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, how does the loose skin under a sea otter's left armpit help the animal?

options.text: It acts like a thick blubber layer that warms the otter's whole body.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 states that sea otters do not have blubber at all and rely on thick fur for warmth; the armpit fold in Paragraph 3 is a carrying pocket.

options.text: It forms a pouch where the otter can store its favorite rock and carry extra clams to the surface.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that loose folds of skin under the sea otter's left armpit form a deep pocket that holds its favorite rock and extra clams from dive to dive.

options.text: It works like a fin that lets the otter swim faster than seals and whales.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 calls the loose skin a 'built-in tool bag' and 'deep pocket' for holding rocks and clams, not a swimming fin.

options.text: It ties the otter to giant kelp blades while the animal sleeps at night.
options.childFeedback: Otters drape long kelp ribbons across their bellies in Paragraph 4 when they sleep; they don't tie kelp with their armpit pouch.

questions.provingSentenceText: Loose folds of skin under the left armpit form a deep pocket that can hold a favorite rock from dive to dive.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that loose folds of skin under the sea otter's left armpit form a deep pocket that holds its favorite rock and extra clams from dive to dive.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that loose folds of skin under the left armpit form a deep pocket used to store a favorite rock tool and carry extra clams to the surface.
questions.retryHint: Read the second and third sentences of Paragraph 3 to see the two things a sea otter tucks into its armpit pocket.

options.text: It compares the weight of a flat anvil stone with the weight of a purple sea urchin.
options.childFeedback: Anvil stones and sea urchins are discussed in Paragraph 2, whereas Paragraph 4 is all about how sea otters rest safely on the water.

options.text: It lists every kind of fish and crab that lives inside the Pacific kelp forest in alphabetical order.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 never lists types of fish or crabs; it describes how sleeping otters wrap themselves in giant kelp and hold paws.

options.text: It describes the problem of ocean currents sweeping sleeping otters away and explains how otters solve it by wrapping in kelp.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 uses a problem-and-solution structure: it explains the danger of strong currents sweeping a sleeping otter out to sea, and then shows how otters solve it by wrapping in kelp ribbons.

options.text: It argues that people should stop visiting rocky beaches along the Pacific coast.
options.childFeedback: The passage never mentions human visitors on beaches or argues against visiting the coast.

questions.provingSentenceText: To stay in one spot, otters drape long ribbons of floating giant kelp across their bellies like seat belts.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 uses a problem-and-solution structure: it explains the danger of strong currents sweeping a sleeping otter out to sea, and then shows how otters solve it by wrapping in kelp ribbons.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 uses a Problem/Solution structure: it introduces the risk of ocean currents sweeping sleeping otters out to sea, and explains how otters solve this by wrapping themselves in giant kelp.
questions.retryHint: Compare the problem described in the second sentence of Paragraph 4 with what otters do in the third and fourth sentences.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why are sea otters important to the health of the giant kelp forest?

options.text: They plant new kelp seeds in the mud whenever they dive to the bottom.
options.childFeedback: Sea otters dive to the bottom to hunt crabs, clams, and urchins (Paragraph 2); they do not plant kelp seeds in the mud.

options.text: They eat large numbers of sea urchins that would otherwise chew through the kelp stems and destroy the forest.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 explains that hungry sea urchins chew through the bottom stems of giant kelp and can wipe out whole underwater forests, so otters protect the kelp by eating thousands of urchins every week.

options.text: They use flat stones to build rock walls that block cold waves from hitting the kelp.
options.childFeedback: Otters carry a single flat stone on their chests to crack shells (Paragraph 2), not to build underwater rock walls against waves.

options.text: They shed thick fur that feeds all the crabs and seals living near the reef.
options.childFeedback: Crabs and seals do not eat sea otter fur; Paragraph 5 says otters protect the green kelp canopy that shelters fish, crabs, and seals.

questions.provingSentenceText: By eating thousands of urchins every week, sea otters play a vital role in protecting the green kelp canopy for fish, crabs, and seals.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 5 explains that hungry sea urchins chew through the bottom stems of giant kelp and can wipe out whole underwater forests, so otters protect the kelp by eating thousands of urchins every week.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 5 explains that sea urchins chew through the bottom stems of giant kelp, and by eating thousands of urchins each week, sea otters protect the kelp canopy.
questions.retryHint: Read the second, third, and fourth sentences of Paragraph 5 to see what sea urchins do to giant kelp and how sea otters stop them.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "This dense fur traps a layer of dry air right against their skin as they swim."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains how dense fur keeps an otter's skin dry and warm, not how otters protect the kelp forest.

options.text: "Most ocean hunters cannot bite through the tough armor of a clam or urchin without breaking their teeth."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 2 explains why clams and urchins are hard to bite open, without showing how eating urchins saves the kelp.

options.text: "The otter also tucks extra clams into this pouch so it can carry several snacks to the surface at once."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 3 describes how an otter carries extra clams in its armpit pouch, rather than how otters help the kelp forest survive.

options.text: "By eating thousands of urchins every week, sea otters play a vital role in protecting the green kelp canopy for fish, crabs, and seals."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by stating that eating thousands of urchins every week is how sea otters protect the green kelp canopy.

questions.provingSentenceText: By eating thousands of urchins every week, sea otters play a vital role in protecting the green kelp canopy for fish, crabs, and seals.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by stating that eating thousands of urchins every week is how sea otters protect the green kelp canopy.
